proposed_edges.relationship: McKay's historical work is Gramscian by his own account: cultural hegemony in The Quest of the Folk (1994), and 'the Gramscian assumptions that have shaped my outlook' (2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: McKay's own words, read in full ("A Note on 'Region' in Writing the History of Atlantic Canada", Acadiensis 29:2, 2000, p. 89): 'the Gramscian assumptions that have shaped my outlook'. Muise (Acadiensis 27:2, 1998, read pp. 124, 128–132) reports that in The Quest of the Folk McKay places himself 'within a neo-marxist framework associated with the work of Antonio Gramsci' and quotes the book (p. 306): 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics'. Wright (Acadiensis 24:2, 1995, p. 132 n. 29): 'For a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian see Ian McKay, The Quest of the Folk'. Critic: Palmer (2009) argues that McKay's Gramsci conflates hegemony and domination. The Quest of the Folk is given through these readers. Distinct from edge_844 (Gramsci → the liberal order framework, 2000): this arrow carries the influence on McKay's work from 1994, before the prospectus.
